summary:
A 96-wide row of eight 12×14 plots facing a gravel lane, with a lantern post on each plot line. Four small pier-raised houses (a front-gable shotgun, a side-gable saddlebag duplex with a central chimney, a hall-and-parlour with an end chimney, and a mirrored shotgun) each have their own wood and tin colour and a porch on the lane. They are followed by a fenced kitchen garden, a chicken coop with its run, a well yard with a shade tree, and a false-front company store. Together they read as a cotton-mill village. One 96x19 row of eight 12-wide modules along a gravel lane: a shotgun house, a saddlebag duplex, a hall-and-parlour cottage, a mirrored shotgun variant, a kitchen garden, a chicken coop, a well yard and a false-front company store. Each has its own wood, roof tin, brick or stone piers, porch and brick chimney with a signal campfire; side columns are fences so plots tile.
elements.md and plan.md (PALETTE, VOCABULARY, ROOMS, PARTS, CHECKLIST, NOTES) are written. Six trade-cut parts.

concept_subject: A sunny Southern cotton-mill village street around 1900: a straight dirt-and-gravel lane with wheel ruts runs left to right, a lantern on a spruce post at every plot line, and eight modules side by side behind low picket and post fences, each with a gate at its middle. From left: a narrow cream birch-clapboard shotgun house with its gable to the lane, set on red-brick piers with fence-lattice skirting, a light-grey tin roof, a small shed-roofed front porch with white posts, a two-leaf front door and dark shutters on the sides, and a brick chimney with a dark band rising beside the east eave and sending up a thin plume of smoke. Next, a brown spruce board-and-batten saddlebag duplex with its long side to the lane, two front doors under one long porch, a rusty red tin roof, and a fat brick chimney standing up through the middle of the ridge. Then a honey-oak clapboard hall-and-parlour cottage with white corner boards, paired windows either side of the door, a porch across the front, a dark wood-shingle side-gable roof and a brick chimney on its west gable end. Then the shotgun again, mirrored, in pinkish-tan jungle wood with dark trim, pale shutters, a green-painted tin roof and its chimney on the west side. Then a fenced kitchen garden: rows of wheat, carrots, potatoes and beetroot on dark farmland, a water channel across the middle with a plank footbridge on the centre path, a composter, a rain barrel and a pumpkin-headed hay scarecrow. Then a small spruce chicken coop on cobble piers with a tiny gable roof, a chicken ramp, and hay and barrel nesting boxes inside, in front of a fenced run with a feed trough and a water tub. Then an open yard with a round cobblestone well under a little oak roof with a hanging lantern, a plank bench, a big leafy oak tree over grassy and podzol patches, and a wash line of white and pale-blue sheets on a fence rail. Last, the company store: a dark-brown plank building whose cream-painted false front rises flat and stepped above its low grey tin roof, with a dark bracketed cornice and the word STORE in black banner letters, two big shop windows, a glazed double door, a shed-roofed porch on posts with a hanging MILL CO sign and lanterns, and inside a counter, stacked shelves, barrels and crates, plus a composter, smoker, loom and fletching table. Lanterns glow under every porch.
